label: Verve
rationale: The summit meeting of three giants — Dizzy Gillespie, Sonny Rollins, and Sonny Stitt — captured in a single December 1957 jam session at Nola Studios. The album embodies the hard-bop cutting session at its most joyful and competitive: a 14-minute “The Eternal Triangle” where Rollins and Stitt trade choruses over a blistering rhythm section, a blues-drenched “After Hours”, and the sunny title track. Penguin Guide 3-star, AllMusic 4-star. Cited as one of the great jam-session records in the jazz catalog. Dizzy Gillespie — the co-inventor of bebop and a defining voice in hard bop — is not yet represented in the canon, a clear gap this album fills.

tracks.title: On the Sunny Side of the Street

personnel_record.notes: Single session December 19, 1957 at Nola Penthouse Sound Studios (Nola Recording Studio), NYC. Cover photography: Burt Goldblatt. Liner notes: Nat Hentoff. Engineer not documented in available sources.

scope_check.boundary_note: Recorded 1957-12-19, released 1959 — comfortably inside 1940–1979, and no opened-gate (free/fusion/ECM) boundary is in play. The only flag: Dizzy's name brushes the pure-bebop exclusion ('Gillespie small groups'), but this date's organizing idiom is a 1957 hard-bop cutting session, not bebop itself — both references examined the flag and agree it does not bite. Noted so John sees it; not a scope_call.

ballot.case_for: Session gravity is the dominant signal: a single fully-documented December 1957 date at Nola (S1–S3) putting Dizzy, a prime Sonny Rollins, and Sonny Stitt in one room is exactly the personnel network this canon exists to surface. 'The Eternal Triangle' — the 14:10 Rollins–Stitt duel over rhythm changes — is a benchmark of tenor lineage, among the most-studied saxophone confrontations in the idiom (Reference 2 calls it legendary in jazz pedagogy; Reference 1 calls it a known touchstone). The record fills a real gap: the co-inventor of bebop is absent from a post-bebop canon, and this is the right shape of Dizzy — a post-bop hard-bop date, not the pure-bebop small-group record the rubric excludes. Discovery value is high: joyful, competitive, with Dizzy's vocal 'Sunny Side of the Street' opening into Rollins' entrance — it plays cold.
ballot.case_against: The critical-consensus evidence sits a tier below the canon's core: Penguin 3-star (not core collection) and AllMusic 4-star, with the Penguin claim in the rationale unattached to any cited source and 4 of 6 dossier sources pure metadata — no DownBeat, canon-list, or canonical-reissue-program attestation (Reference 1's strongest point). It is not a defining statement for any of its three leads: Dizzy's canonical records lie elsewhere, Rollins has Saxophone Colossus and beyond, and Stitt's most-argued showcases are elsewhere. Structurally it is a Norman Granz blowing session — two long blues, a rhythm-changes contrafact, two standards — leaning on solo sparring over stock forms rather than album-level vision, and its historical draw belongs mostly to the Rollins–Stitt confrontation rather than to Gillespie as leader (Reference 2's attribution point).
ballot.disagreement: None on the verdict — both references independently reached contested / strong. The genuine split is over which against-case is load-bearing: Reference 1 weights the thin, metadata-heavy sourcing and the unattached Penguin claim as what blocks consensus_core, while Reference 2 weights the blowing-session architecture and the diluted Gillespie leadership (the record's identity is the Rollins–Stitt duel). Reference 2 also credits 'The Eternal Triangle' with legendary pedagogical-lineage weight that Reference 1 treats as real but modest.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes John give Sonny Side Up a listen at strong priority and rule on whether unmatched session gravity and the Dizzy-shaped gap outweigh good-but-not-core critical consensus and jam-session architecture.
